author: reek
body: A runnable model of triplanar-mapped terrain with height-blended layers. A world position goes in, a lit surface colour comes out.

author: reek
body: It cites both earlier waves, which is the pattern this library has settled into rather than an accident: `OceanModel` carries the Real math kernel and `V3`, `CloudModel` carries the lattice noise, the fractal sum, and `c-remap`. Each wave adds only what it genuinely needs that no earlier one had, and whole-program dead-code elimination drops the rest. Terrain adds a RIDGED fractal sum, the triplanar projection itself, and the height blend.

author: reek
body: The noise is three-dimensional and the terrain is a function of two coordinates, so the sample point rides the y = 0 plane. That is not a workaround: a slice of a 3-D lattice noise is a perfectly good 2-D noise, and reusing one implementation is worth more than a second one that only takes two arguments.

author: reek
body: The normal by central differences. The cross product of the two tangents of a heightfield reduces to this, and taking the difference across the sample rather than forward from it keeps the normal centred on the point it belongs to.

author: reek
body: The epsilon is a real parameter and not a formality. Too small and the difference is lost in the noise of the fractal sum; too large and the normal is an average over ground the shading is not standing on.

author: reek
body: The blend weights. Each is how much the surface faces that axis, raised to a sharpness and normalised so the three sum to one.

author: reek
body: The pattern being projected. A procedural fractal sum stands in for what would be a texture read on a GPU; the projection is the same either way, and the point of the model is the projection.

author: reek
body: A material is a colour and a height. The height is what the blend competes on, and it is why this is not a lerp.

author: reek
body: The blend. Add each material's height to its weight, take the larger, and cut a threshold a fixed depth below it; whatever still stands above the threshold contributes in proportion.

author: reek
body: The consequence is that at an equal 50/50 weight the two materials do NOT produce an even mix. Wherever material A's height texture is locally higher it wins outright, and wherever B's is, B does, so the boundary becomes an interlocking edge with the shape of the height textures rather than a straight soft band. `terrain-splat-width` sets how wide the contested zone is: at zero the transition is a hard cut following the height fields, and widening it fades the edge back toward a lerp.

author: reek
body: The surface. Two blends, not one: rock against grass by SLOPE, and then snow against that result by ALTITUDE. Both use the same operator, which is the point -- the technique composes.

author: reek
body: Slope comes from the normal's y component directly, which is the cosine of the ground's tilt. Grass on shallow ground, rock where it steepens, and the height blend puts the grass into the rock's hollows instead of drawing a contour line between them.

author: reek
body: Lambert against the sun plus a flat sky ambient. Deliberately plain: the subject of this wave is what colour the surface IS, and a more elaborate light would only make it harder to see whether the projection and the blend are right.

author: reek
body: The field. Frequency is per metre, so it is small; amplitude is in metres.

author: reek
body: The splat. Depth is how much a material's height counts against its weight; width is how wide the contested zone is.

author: reek
body: The scale of the height texture the blend competes on.

author: reek
body: These three numbers, and the two ramp widths below, are the whole of the TERRACING problem, which is worth setting down in full because the first four attempts at it were wrong.

author: reek
body: The symptom was stair-step contours across every slope. Two experiments located it, and they are the useful part: rendering with a CONSTANT albedo gave a perfectly smooth surface, which clears the height field, the normals, and the march; rendering with the blends intact but FLAT material colours kept the terraces, which clears the colour textures. What was left was the blend itself.

author: reek
body: The mechanism, once cornered, is arithmetic. A material wins where `weight + depth * height` is larger, so the boundary lies where the difference crosses zero. The weights here are slope and altitude, which vary smoothly and slowly, so their zero crossing is a smooth contour of the terrain -- a terrace -- unless the height term is large enough to push the crossing around. A 2-octave normalised sum sits in roughly [0.35, 0.65], so at the original depth of 0.5 it moved the boundary by about +/-0.15 against weights spanning the full [-1, 1]. Far too little.

author: reek
body: The last piece is the ramps: `terrain-slope-lo/hi` and `terrain-snow-lo/hi` were originally wide enough that most of the landscape sat permanently in the contested zone, so the blend mottled everything instead of acting at a boundary. Narrowing them puts most ground decisively in one material and leaves the blend a thin band to work in, which is where an interlocking edge is worth having.

author: reek
body: This chapter is a library and carries no entry point, for the same reason `OceanModel` and `CloudModel` carry none: a chapter with an `opening` cannot be cited by a program that has its own.

author: reek
body: `TerrainSamples` reports the field and the blends at chosen points. `TerrainRender` raymarches the heightfield into an image.
